utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, good morning to you. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. For the record, all the accused are here. From the Defence teams I notice the absence of Mr. Ostojic, Mr. Lazarevic, Madam Nikolic and Mr. Haynes. Is Mr. Krgovic here? Because I can't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: He's not, Your Honour. This is Nikola Krgovic who has not been in the courtroom before. He's keeping an eye on me on behalf of his father.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My father would have been very proud of me if I had ever decided and accepted to do that. But I never went. From the Prosecution we have Mr. McCloskey, Ms. Soljan and Mr. Elderkin. The witness is already present. Mr. Zivanovic, if you could cut it short, please, because we have actually -- went far and wide outside the parameters that we had set, in spite of our instructions and directions, both you and the witness continued to practically ignore them completely except for the reference to the Vuga report. Otherwise we have got beyond the real meaning, the definition of these four terms which should have been covered in ten minutes. Yes, good morning, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Forca. You have heard that we were requested to shorten your examination. Please tell us which sources in the English language you have drawn upon to formulate your positions on the appropriate terms to be used for these four Serb expressions?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, while preparing for my testimony, I used the Morton Benson dictionary, the English-Serbian/Serbian-English dictionary. I used a NATO dictionary, NATO glossary of terms and definitions, AP 6. [In English] From 2007.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1-02, Department of Defence Dictionary of Military and Associated Terms. From 2005, [Interpretation] I have also used instructions from the US [In English] Armed Forces from 2003. [Interpretation] I've used instructions from England, command from 1995. I've used instructions from the US of A [In English] AFM 3-0, from February 2008. [Interpretation] I've used instructions [In English] Joint operation from the USA. [Interpretation] I've used American instructions from [In English] staff organisation and operations FM 101-5. And army planning and orders AFM 5-0. [Interpretation] Since we are in Holland I've also used the instructions of the Royal Dutch Army of the land forces command and control from the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell us what the -- which appropriate English word did you use for the term "komandovanje"?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, according to all the Serbian language dictionaries and encyclopedias, the adequate term for the English term "command" is "komandovanje" in the Serbian language. I don't think that can be in any way contested.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since this is not a term at issue, I would like you to tell us, with regard to the term "control" that was used in the NATO documents you perused in the English language and that's in relation to the Serbian term of "rukovodjenje"?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say first what the American language 1-02 says about "komandovanje" and then I will get back to your question. It says that the authority that the commander in legal terms exercises over his subordinates based on his rank. "Komandovanje," "command," implies competence and efficiency in the use of available resources. And mark this, for planning the use of forces, organising, directing, coordination and control. In practical terms, these are the functions of "rukovodjenje." When I told you last Friday that I stayed in numerous countries at various conferences, we were particularly interested in the process of planning and "kontrola." In that sense, NATO uses the guidelines for operation and planning which are of great interest to us, as well as the instructions for the control of operative abilities of the armed forces which we've also used in our work. In answer to Mr. Zivanovic's question, when it comes to the term "control" in English, the NATO dictionary, AAP 6, the basic meaning is that of the competence of the commander for part of the activities of the -- of subordinates or other organisations that are not under his command and which cover the responsibility for the execution of orders or directives. Another important matter, which the text also refers to, is the competence as a whole or in part may be transferred or delegated. A dictionary from the United States, 1-02, states that the basic meaning of "control" in English is a competence which can be less than the full command authority exercised by a commander over a part of the activities of his subordinates or other organisations. Your Honours, the main problem in the translation of the terms "rukovodjenje" and "komandovanje," "command" and "control," arises precisely when we come to the term of "control," because this term, in its more immediate meaning, in fact means to check, to control, to ascertain the state of affairs, which is equivalent to the term of "kontrola" in the B/C/S, in the Serbian language. Now, when it comes to the compound expression of "command and control," when you analyse that expression, you find that the term of "control" has a broader meaning as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain this part now that you've come to broach it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, for this particular topic, I used the documents of the land forces of the Dutch Royal Army, of the United States and of the United Kingdom, all of which interpret the term of "control" in English in a similar way, and that's to say in the syntagm of command and control. I will now explain what the term of "control" and the scope of use of that word, how it is defined in these documents. In the document called, "Command and control" of the land forces of the Dutch army, "Control" is to -- means to produce documents and orders based on a decision taken, the conveyance of plans and orders to those involved in the operation, supervision of the execution of the operation, inspection or the controlling of the operation, and the execution of the operation as needed and pursuant to additional orders. Now, the manual, "joint operation, 3-0" from the United States defines the term of "control" as -- or rather defines the term of "command and control" so as to include the receiving and transmitting of information, situation assessment in the immediate environment, preparation of plans and orders, command over the subordinate forces, setting up of the headquarters of a command post, coordination and control of lethal and non-lethal powers, coordination and integration of the support by a joint multi-national organisations, governmental organisations and non-governmental organisations, as well as the public relation activities in the area of activity. Of particular importance to my expert opinion was the American instruction, command and control, FM 6-0, which in its preamble states that up until World War II, there existed only the notion of command without control. In the aftermath of World War II, command expanded to include command and control. The conclusion of the authors of that instruction is that the notion of command and control was present and familiar in the area of the land forces, but was not interpreted correctly. The land forces have struggled to arrive at a definition that would define in precise terms what the duties and activities of a commander are. And whatever the commander does comes under the term of command. What the staff does together with the commander falls under the term of control. The definition of the expression "command and control" in that dictionary, FN 6-0 is as follows: Command and control is the exercise of the rights and competences by a given commander over the forces assigned to him or attached to him with a view to a successful accomplishment of a mission. The commander exercises command through a situ system. Your Honours, I have photographs with me, the necessary diagrams, and all the documents that I've referred to I have here, and if you want me to, I can ask that this diagram be placed on the ELMO and I can explain as much as I've been explaining to you now with regards to the expression of "command and control."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections, any objections from anyone? Yes, Mr. Elderkin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Again, I'm not sure how this relates to the translation issue. I think that we would like to know what "rukovodjenje" means and "komandovanje," but expression of the NATO system of command and control is way outside the scope of what we are here for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But hope springs eternal, if you wait a few more hours, perhaps you can get to that. Yes, we can -- I suggest that it's put on the ELMO so that we can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: These documents are at our list and as far as I know they are in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They are in e-court. And then we can upload it on e-court if you give us the reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Also, could we have an exhibit number for this, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll find it. It is 1D1181.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. I think I found it at 1D1183 on page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this what you wanted to explain?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, you can see the command and control system from the American instruction FM 6-0. I'm going to try and explain this image by starting from the bottom of it. In order for a mission to be accomplished, where it says "mission accomplishment" which need to be exercised by the forces as the object, there is an ongoing planning, preparation and execution, and also an ongoing assessment and reassessment. The essence of the control process is the command operational picture or as we would translate that into Serbian, the common operational picture of the theatre of war, or the zone of operations, for the commander or -- and his staff. This is exercised through the elements of the system of command and control, and the elements are the personnel, equipment and others, facilities, procedures and the IT management. All of this is in the hands of the commander who is the leader, who is the person who passes decisions. This is our understanding of the command and control system. I would like to ask for your attention and I would like to draw your attention to a different page in the same document. The page number is 3-4. Could this please be put on the ELMO or displayed otherwise?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: 1184, I believe. No, no. No, sorry. It is just the second page of the same exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, correct, correct. [Interpretation] Your Honours, the title of this image is, "Control functions of the command and control system," depicts the three key functions with the groups of tasks which all fall under the control function of the command and control system. The first one would be support achieving situational understanding. The second one, regulate forces and operating systems. And the third one, allow the organisation to adapt to change. The activities undertaken by the staff within the aforementioned functions are to determine and dynamically adapt needs to collect, analyse, display, safeguard and convey information and to envisage possible threats within the duration of the execution. When it comes to the regulation of forces, the main tasks are support the commander's decision making, to define limits, to allocate resources to requirements and tasks, to direct operations by producing and disseminating orders, to acquire means to accomplish the mission, to develop specific directives from general guidance. Under the third function, the following tasks may be seen, the first one to forecast change in friendly, enemy or environmental situations, to identify variances in performance from the concept operations and to report significant changes in the situation to the commander. Your Honours, thank you very much for allowing me to present these illustrations. And now, if we are arriving at a conclusion about the terms of "command and control," we said that "command" is the same thing as "komandovanje." "Control" however may be translated in the Serbian language both as "kontrola," which is assessment of the situation, and also implicitly, not explicitly, mind you, as "rukovodjenje." In other words, in the Serbian language, "komandovanje" and "rukovodjenje" may be translated into English as "command" and "control." However, in order to avoid any confusion, in terms of control containing control, for example, and I'm going to draw a parallel when we say fruit salad in the Serbian language, that term contains pears, apples, cherries, and fruit salad which doesn't make any sense. It is logically incorrect. And in that sense, as I've already said, on Friday, the terms are coined on a scientific basis but also they result from conventions that have been adopted. In my view here, we have to go by convention in order to avoid confusion among people. And this would be my proposal, based on my experience, based on my insight, into documents that the term "komandovanje" and "rukovodjenje" in Serbian be translated into English as "command" and "control." But in brackets, "(as managing)," closed brackets. For the control or control in the Serbian language to be translated into English as "control." And then in brackets, there should be the word "check" or "checking".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Just to be clear, this is, I think, what Mr. McCloskey agreed to on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's my recollection, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you something else, when it comes to professional control can you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Your Honours, as I already said on Friday, expert control does not exist as a term, "strucno rukovodjenje" derives from two different terms: "strucan," "expert"; "rukovoditi," "control." In those terms, the adequate word in the Serbian of "strucan" would be "expert" or "skilled" which implies that an expert would be a more appropriate term because skill is something that has to do with dexterity in performing manual tasks. Since we have already established that commands have expert organs which are involved in expert control, which means that it is the experts who manage -- now when it comes to the term "strucan" in the Serbian language, the English equivalent of that would be expert, specialist and authority. In view of all that has been said so far, my proposal would be that the term "strucno rukovodjenje" in the Serbian language would be translated into English as "specialist managing."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We would like to tender all documents from our list but all these documents were not shown to the witness. He referred to that. And if it is necessary, I would put all of these documents to him if it is necessary for tendering.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: That seems entirely unnecessary, in view of, partly Your Honour's direction that the witness would present his evidence orally but it seems unnecessary on the basis of the explanations he has given us for each of the four terms. And we are not learning about NATO doctrine here. We are asking about the meaning of words as used in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't think we ought to lose more time on this, and without the need of you referring the documents to the witness, again it will save us time, we are admitting for whatever relevance or importance they may have in due course all the documents that you indicated, except the report, obviously, except the report, and they are being admitted from the bar table. Thank you. So have you finished?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honours. [Interpretation] Thank you. I have finished my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Nikolic, do you have a cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you, we don't have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Mr. Gosnell?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: No questions, Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, in the light of the Trial Chamber's ruling on Friday at 22572, we have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Sarapa?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So Mr. Elderkin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And also none from us, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. That's a very practical approach, all of you, I think considering the situation, how it has developed and we could have sent Mr. Forca back home even Friday, if you had heeded our advice. General, it was a pleasure meeting you here in the Trial Chamber. We learned a lot from what you came here to explain to us. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I wish to thank you for having come over. And on behalf of everyone present, I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Zivanovic, any other document, apart from the ones that we have admitted from the bar table?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we don't have any documents. And we can start with the next witness. Who is your next witness? I just want to make sure that we've got the right person indicated today.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good morning. Our next witness is Nebojsa Micic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I'll be leading that witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's my understanding this witness is here to talk about a subject we've some about before, a post-war investigation into Mr. Obrenovic taking tractors or boats. My information is that this matter was never adjudicated or finalised or resolved in any way at the time, so I imagine here that it may have some relevance, but I would hope that we don't -- some of the time frames are pretty long for something we've heard about already with -- I don't understand the real relevance here but -- so I just bear that in mind unless there is something else that I'm not being told about this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes -- Madam Tapuskovic, would you like to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to comment, but I would need to go into private session for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime, Madam Tapuskovic, line 5 on page 14, there is a reference to Rule 69. Did you mean Rule 68?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I mentioned Rule 65 ter and the summaries submitted thereunder. I wasn't following the transcript when I was addressing the Trial Chamber. I said that the brief summary of the testimony this witness ought to give was contained in the 65 ter filing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have the break now, 25 minutes. Thank you. --- Break taken at 9.52 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir, and welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have been summoned as a Defence witness by the team defending Colonel Popovic in this case. Before you start giving evidence, our rules require that you make a solemn declaration that you will be testifying the truth. Madam Usher is going to hand you the text of the solemn declaration which you're kindly asked to read out loud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Micic. Make yourself -- please make yourself comfortable. You are going to be asked first questions by Madam Tapuskovic, who is appearing for Colonel Popovic and she will then be followed by others. Madam Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Micic, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me introduce myself to you. My name is Mira Tapuskovic and as the Presiding Judge said, I am a member of the Defence team for Mr. Popovic. Kindly answer my questions slowly so that your answer may be entered correctly into the transcript. To allow for this, you have to make a short pause before answering my question so that my question can first be interpreted and entered into the transcript. First, tell us your full name.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: Nebojsa Micic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us the place and year of your birth.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: Zemun, the 2nd of May, 1959.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us something about your educational background.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: I graduated from the military high school and the military academy for the land forces and the security school in Pancevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When did you first take up a post?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us where did your career take you from 1977?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: I worked for four years as a platoon -- as a tank platoon commander upon completion of my high school. After that, I enlisted into the security school and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The security service, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and I have spent my career in the security service until my retirement on various duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When were you retired?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: In the month of February 2002.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: During your service in the security organs where you said you spent most of your career, can you tell us which duties you performed?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: The first duty I performed was the security desk officer in a regiment. Then a security desk officer in a brigade. Next, I was the chief of security of a brigade. I had the latter duty until 1987. That was still before the breakout of the conflict. Next, I was assistant chief for security of a corps, and I was in charge of counter-intelligence affairs for a short while. After that, I was the chief of security of a corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us which corps that was?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: The 7th Corps, stationed in -- or rather based in Trebinje first and then in Bileca. The next duty I took up was in the security administration, where I was first the desk officer for anti-terrorist combat and anti-constitutional activity. Later on, I became the chief of the anti-terrorist and anti-constitutional activity department in that same administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us what you were doing when the 1991 events occurred in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: At that time, I was in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: Once the units of the former JNA withdrew, I was transferred to the Kraljevo garrison. Quite soon, or two months later, I was transferred to the Banja Luka garrison, to the tank brigade of that garrison.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where is Kraljevo?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: In Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that this took place several months later. Can you recall specifically which year that was when you became the member of the armoured brigade in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: On the 29th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As you say, you stayed there until the month of April 1997?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you spent your entire service in the security organ. Can you tell us which regulations you applied in your work?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: We had regulations that specifically applied to us. We had both military and civilian life regulations applicable to us. From civilian regulations, we applied the relevant provisions of the Criminal Code, of the law on criminal procedure, whereas the military regulations governed security affairs, either in the more general rules of service or in the more specific regulations governing the security organs. The security organs had their own internal rules. Therefore --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, it's not clear what time period we are talking about and it's not really even clear which army we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that when he went to Kraljevo, he was still JNA. That I -- I think that is clear enough to me. But after that, when you were transferred to Banja Luka and then in relation to the events that have just been put to you by Ms. Tapuskovic, I think the question that -- or the point made by Mr. McCloskey is very relevant and you need to tell us exactly when, what time frame you're referring to, and whether you're talking of the JNA or the VRS.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was referring to the regulations that I adhered to, as well as the service I worked for. Until new regulations were adopted, we complied with the regulations or laws that were in force. For instance, before the laws, relevant laws in Republika Srpska were adopted in 1994, we applied the legislation of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is simply non-responsive to your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. You haven't answered the question. Previously, Madam Tapuskovic, in reacting to your previous statement that you were then transferred to the armoured brigade in Banja Luka, pointed out to you that you stayed there until the month of April 1997. And she asked you, then, which regulations you applied to your work, and you started giving an answer. But we are talking of a long period of time, so we need to know exactly when you were referring to the various provisions of the Criminal Code and the rest, what period of time you were referring to, and whether at, at the time, which army you belonged to, whether it was the VRS, whether it was the JNA and then the VRS, whether it was the Serbian army. You need to specify this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me answer this specifically. Until 1992, when the former JNA withdrew from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I was a member of the Yugoslav People's Army. After that, I remained of my own free will a member of the army of Republika Srpska. And I remained a member of the army of Republika Srpska until I was retired in 2002. As far as the regulations are concerned, we applied the regulations I previously referred to in our work. What needs to be kept in mind is that the regulations changed over time but before the SFRY Criminal Code ceased to be applied, we continued to apply it. Of course, when the Republika Srpska Criminal Code was adopted in 1994, we started applying those. Whatever the case was, whichever legislation was in force, we applied it until new legislation was adopted. Now, we had our internal rules of the security organ, which defined our purview and methods of work, and these did not change until after the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Micic, I will have to ask you to speak more slowly because it is difficult to enter everything you say into the transcript. Does this mean, what you've just said, that until certain regulations of the army of Republika Srpska were passed, the JNA regulations were in force as well as the legislation that was in force in Yugoslavia at the time?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As a member of that service of the security organ, which duties did you discharge?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: Just as any other security officer, I had to comply with the rules which defined our purview. There were two sets of tasks.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us which these two sets of tasks were?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: Counter-intelligence tasks and the so-called staff security tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could just perhaps get whether he's in a brigade or a corps and what year we are talking about during the war, during this time, just a little bit more. We are in a real vacuum here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Could you pinpoint these to us, please, Mr. Micic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can answer, and if your question is about the war, I was the chief of security in a brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What brigade and what time precisely are we talking about -- or you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the armoured brigade in Banja Luka of the 1st Krajina Corps. I joined that brigade in December 1991, and I stayed with it until April 1997. That's how long I was in that particular position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, to provide some further clarification and to answer the Trial Chamber's question, whether the tasks of the security organs are the same irrespective of the unit, whether it is a brigade or a corps?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: The tasks of a security organ differ at different levels. The higher the level, the more specialised the tasks are. You can notice that from my career path that I described at the beginning, but when we are talking about a regiment, brigade and battalion, all the security organs perform two types of tasks. The first set of tasks are counter-intelligence tasks and the other group of tasks are staff security tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, I would object to any further discussion. We have 20 hours down for Mr. Vuga who is a security officer and he's going to go -- this officer is going to go into what a security officer does and this whole counter-intelligence thing, we are going to get in this -- in a repetitive cumulative thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Tapuskovic, Mr. McCloskey is 100 per cent right. Actually, this witness, according to the summary that you have provided, will be testifying to events that relate or go back to the time when he was officer in the security organ of the VRS Main Staff in 1998 and 1999. So why don't you go there straight away and forget what was the position when he was in the regiment in Banja Luka, which concluded, finished in 1997, anyway. Go straight to the subject matter that you brought this witness to testify upon.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're absolutely right, Your Honours, and this was going to be my last background question. And I wish to be moving on to a different period and talk about more concrete things.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Micic, do you know and what do you know about the operative subject Kum?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: The operative subject Kum was a subject that was relative to the abuse of office in the sector of the Zvornik Brigade or the so-called 503rd Brigade of the army of Republika Srpska. And it was part of a broader operation known under the name of Komfor [phoen]. And that broader operation also dealt with different types of abuses of office in the units of the army of Republika Srpska across the entire territory covered by the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you dealt with abuses of office, what did that mean at the time, at the level of the operative case?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: This was done with the main goal of curbing the white-collar and property crime which increased during the war and almost went through the roof and started threatening the combat readiness of the units. That's when the operative action was launched, in order to discover the perpetrators of such crimes and to prevent the spreading of this phenomenon in the army of Republika Srpska and to eliminate any consequences of such activities in the units.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. When we are talking about the abuse of power of office that you've just spoken about, what period of time are you talking about? When did the abuse occur?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: This abuse of office occurred during the war, and in the period after the war, obviously. This lasted over a longer period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you said that this particularly concerned the 503rd Brigade of the army of Republika Srpska, what was the previous name of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: Since the names of the units changed, I know it as the 503rd Motorised Brigade, but in unofficial terms it was also known as the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When this Operation Kum was launched, where the headquarters of the brigade was and who was its commander at the time?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: When this Operation Kum was launched, the brigade headquarters was in Zvornik, and its commander was Lieutenant Colonel Dragan Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Micic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like to call up Exhibit number 1D435 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I apologise. We don't have a document with that number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you verify this, Ms. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this document was admitted in October, on the 31st of October 2007, to be more precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah. That may be -- I'm sure that's so but that doesn't mean we have been provided any notice of it. But at this point I'll just withdraw the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see the document, Mr. Micic?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It says, in the left upper corner, that this was drafted by the commander of the 5th Corps, the security department. Can you please tell us, the 5th Corps, what was its previous former name?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: Again, I cannot give you the exact establishment number -- name, but it was known as the Romanija Corps. And when the events were occurring, it was the command of the 5th Corps as it is stated on the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Micic, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When did you see this document for the first time?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: If you are referring to a time frame, I saw this document when I was engaged in this particular case. As it says on the document, the author of the document was the security department of the 5th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm now going to read the first paragraph of the document to you, which states, "In order to prove and document the suspicions that Kum is one of the persons who is a member of a group engaged in criminal activities against the army of Republika Srpska, this department, upon the order and in cooperation with the security administration of the General Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, on the 20th of June, 1999, embarked on the activities to elucidate the case."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: This was a sight translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the first paragraph that I've just read out to you, the word, "Kum" has been used and it is in inverted commas. Can you please tell us who this term referred to at the time?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: The word "Kum" referred to Dragan Obrenovic, Lieutenant Dragan Obrenovic, and this would be a customary code name that is normally used in the documents of the security organ, and it is used in communication which is not written communication, and I'm talking about telephone and other similar types of communication.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Why would you use a code name?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: As I've already told you, a code name would be assigned to a certain person in order to be able to communicate, to allow for the communication between the security organs in order to avoid using the real name.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Who gave this name to this operation?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: I was the one who chose this code name for this particular operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It arises from the first paragraph that I have just read out to you that on the 26 -- 20th of June, 1999, the activities were launched in order to elucidate the case. Tell me, please, this task, did it have a preceding period, a period leading up to it?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a period leading up to the Operation Kum. I can't tell you exactly to what extent the security organs of the 503rd Brigade and the corps security organ worked on collecting information to launch this operation. I can only tell you how much I was involved in the case. I can't tell you how long were they involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what was your role in this operation, the Operation Kum?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: My role in this case was to coordinate and assist the subordinated security organs, and in this particular case, it was the security organ of the 5th Corps, and the 503rd Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So you were providing specialist assistance, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And let us now remind ourselves, when you joined the 503rd Brigade to work on this operative case, Kum, what was your position at the time and where were you at the time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. He's never stated he joined the 503rd Brigade. That's leading. I can't tell what unit he's a part of from these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Tapuskovic, I think you need to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The witness said that he got the assignment and that he came -- arrived to provide professional assistance and to be coordinator and for that reason I said that when he arrived in the brigade in order to perform this job of coordination and specialist assistant, where had he come from and from what position and I may have put my question a bit awkwardly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Micic? Did you actually join the 503rd Motorised Brigade at the end?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you implied that joining up means becoming part of the establishment, I would say no. I had arrived from the security administration as a temporary assistance and I was in the position that I already mentioned and it was my temporary mission, temporary task, on the order of the Chief of Staff of the security administration of the General Staff of the army. I was there as desk officer for anti-terrorist and anti-constitutional department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's clear enough. Let's proceed, Madam Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At that moment, what phase was the operative case Kum in?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: When I arrived in Zvornik, and I arrived in the unit, this case was in the phase when all the operative information had been collected. This is our jargon. This is a rather low-level. A higher level would be the level when the documentation had -- has been collected and that's why the chief of administration had sent me to coordinate the work and to provide assistance to the subordinated units, in order to move the case from the stage of collecting information into a higher phase which would be either documenting the allegations, confirm the allegations or reject the allegations altogether.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe in very brief terms how did you coordinate and provide specialist assistance to that unit? Did you have to surmount any obstacles in your work or not?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: When I arrived in the Zvornik Brigade, or the 503rd Motorised Brigade, I had a conversation with the commander, Lieutenant Colonel Obrenovic, and the security organ of the 503rd Motorised Brigade, Lieutenant Dragoslav Slavic, was also present during that conversation. I told the brigade commander that I would be spending a certain period of time in the area of responsibility of his unit, and I told him that I would spend a certain period of time in the unit command and on the ground performing some tasks that fall within the purview of the security organ. This was a very short meeting, maybe 15 to 20 minutes, and this was customary for anybody who arrived at a unit. This was just an official meeting, more a protocol matter than anything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that there was -- the stage that lay ahead of you was that of documenting what had been investigated. What waited for you in store there?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: In that stage, I had daily meetings with the security organs of the 503rd Brigade and of the security department of the corps, Lieutenant Colonel Momcilo Pajic, who was the chief of security of the 7th Corps at the time. From the very start, we made an assessment of the situation and the intelligence gathered, produced a work plan for that particular case, designated the persons responsible for certain tasks arising from and dictated by the case at hand. We divided the necessary work amongst ourselves and embarked on a stage where the intelligence gathered would be double-checked and documented, and I'm referring to the intelligence, the information that had been gathered and in existence before my arrival at the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, at the time, did you have information to the effect that Dragan Obrenovic had come by certain knowledge concerning Operation Kum?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: Upon my arrival in the unit, there were certain indications showing that Lieutenant Colonel Dragan Obrenovic was able to learn that the activities investigated would be documented. This because he had for a while beforehand been opening the mail arriving for the 503rd Brigade. There was one such case which had been discovered. He also became resentful and hostile toward the security organ and this manifested itself in such a way that he assigned Lieutenant Dragoslav Savic to conduct anti-personnel tank -- anti-personnel mines drills in the area of Kuslat. He did not provide him with the necessary amount of fuel which he needed to carry out the tasks given to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You say that Dragan Obrenovic -- can you hear me, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's all right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that Dragan Obrenovic opened official mail. Can you tell us what sort of mail this was?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: There was one incident where the official mail addressed to the security organ of the 503rd Motorised Brigade had been opened. The contents of the letters is something that I know nothing of. I only know that he had been opening the mail intended for the security organ of that unit, which was the reason why the superior security officer from the relevant department of the 7th Corps had to intervene. He sent a warning to the commander of the Zvornik Brigade and said that this was an unlawful act on his part, to open the mail intended for the security organ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I would like to know if Lieutenant Dragoslav Savic had already been assigned to conduct anti-personnel tank or mine drills in the area of Kuslat before or by the time that Mr. Micic arrived in Zvornik on this assignment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so. Precisely as you put it. This happened before my arrival there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if that is so, do have you an explanation why the same Savic was present when you had a first meeting with Dragan Obrenovic? Why would he be there present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he was the security chief of that unit. It was only natural for him to accompany me on the meeting with his commander, where I was supposed to inform them of the nature of my stay with that unit. There was nothing out of the ordinary in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it was you who asked Savic to accompany you for that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Madam Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise to you. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If there is anything besides mail opening and sending people out to minefields, this could go on forever, none of which we've had notice from. I mean, what goes on in an army three years after a war between the security branch -- I mean, they have to give us notice. They can't just cruise through this stuff with all this gossipy material. It's just a total waste of time. We are 1998 for God's sake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Tapuskovic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. However, I wanted to make an introduction into the Operation Kum where the subject on investigations and operative activities were certain activities that took place after the war but during the war as well. We will have certain documents to show. Now, can we have shown in e-court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I'm going to have to insist that she make no reference to anything that's happened during the war. We have had no notice of this, this incredible sloppy, unprofessional conduct I've put up with quite a bit and it's just a total waste of time. She's now going to go into the wartime period? I certainly object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What are you going to address with your next series of questions, Madam Tapuskovic? Why don't you -- I've been taught that you should know exactly where you want to go, and go directly there and forget about marginal matters or what could be completely useless or irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have numerous documents speaking to the abuse of office committed in the 503rd Brigade and we have documents showing that the very commander of the brigade, Obrenovic, was involved in that. We wanted to make an introduction into that topic but we can skip that. These are documents that we find very important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you've brought the witness here to testify on the gathering of evidence and what came out of it and that's it. I mean, we are not trying here Dragan Obrenovic for what he might have or not have done before, during and after the war. This is not the purpose why the witness is here. The witness is here to testify on his role in the investigations that he conducted, and that's it. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't object to these documents coming into evidence. I do object to this -- this is an investigator, he can talk about his investigations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- but to go through every one of his investigative documents would not be appropriate for any investigator to testify to and is a waste of time, but he can tell us about the investigation. I have no problem with that and the documents can come into evidence but to go through every document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is precisely what I was saying, Mr. McCloskey. We want to hear what the witness can tell us about his investigations and the outcome of such investigations, if there was an outcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the subject of investigations and intelligence gathering was something -- was in fact the commander of the brigade, Lieutenant Colonel Obrenovic. We will not be going through all the documents but we have to indicate the group, the set of documents that we have, that we will be tendering into evidence. It was for this reason that we wanted to show through the introduction how the witness came to be involved in this operative action.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, did Dragan Obrenovic ever have a word with you after having found out that he was the target of that investigation?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: After that initial meeting where I announced my stay with that unit, and in the course of my work, which effectively lasted some 20 days, Lieutenant Colonel Dragan Obrenovic asked, through the corps commander, General Andric, that I explain to him the true reasons for my stay in his unit. After having observed that I summoned for interviews certain commanding senior officers of his unit, who probably informed him what my interviews with them were about and what sort of questions I put to them, he insisted with the corps commander, on the occasion of a briefing which took place at the headquarters at Vlasenica, where six-monthly briefings of brigade commanders took place, at a -- or rather during an interval at that briefing, he insisted that I explain what that was all about.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned, at page 34, in line 22, General Andric. Can you tell us who General Andric was at the time?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: General Andric was the corps commander, and according to the chain of command he was the first superior to the commander of the Zvornik Brigade, that is to say Lieutenant Colonel Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did Obrenovic take any countermeasures at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: I haven't finished my earlier answer. I accepted the invitation from General Andric and in my contacts with Lieutenant Colonel Dragan Obrenovic, I told him openly that he was the target of an investigation of the security organs. I asked him whether he had any additional questions and very soon thereafter, with the permission of the general, I left the office.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, please answer the question I put to you a moment ago, having learned that he was the target of investigations, did Dragan Obrenovic take any countermeasures?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: As for me personally and the group of people I worked with, he did not take any open measures or actions against us. Whether he did so incovertly [as interpreted], I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did he try to work toward having certain individuals transferred elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that one of the witnesses we got in touch with, and who provided us with a statement about abuse of office, and that was Lieutenant Colonel Dragan Jokic, the chief of engineering of the 503rd Motorised Brigade, he had him transferred to the command of the 5th Corps. There were two or three more officers who were removed, if I can put it that way, at the time and these were officers who disagreed with the method of work employed by Lieutenant Colonel Obrenovic, and I'm referring to the very abuse of office committed.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Micic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have a look at the document, if it's still in e-court? And I'm referring to the same document, 1D435.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection to the use of this document. I think he can use it to refresh his recollection but an investigator's investigative documents are not normally the kind of thing you just plough through like this. He can tell us about it. If he needs to refresh his recollection to it but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I still haven't heard the question. Let's hear the question first.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Micic, the documents you had at your disposal at which you obtained, did they expressly state the extent of abuse of office ascribed to him?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: Yes. I recall a document which contained seven, eight, nine -- nine such sets of problems which tied Lieutenant Colonel Obrenovic with abuse of office. We refer to those documents as the overview of intelligence gathered.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the amount of intelligence and documents was that you had and which incriminated Obrenovic with regard to abuse of office?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: I believe that the dossier amounted to a binder of documents. In other words, there were several documents, briefs, records of interviews, statements taken and other documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the example of office abuse that were listed in the documentation allegedly committed by Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can do that. I remember a car, a Golf, that Lieutenant Colonel Obrenovic used for a while as his vehicle, that was later on sold on to the Zvornik bank and was registered to the name of Mr. Obrenovic. I also remember a tractor --

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please wait for my next question?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now call up 1D406 in e-court, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel. Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Micic, in your binder of documents, when you investigated the abuse of the Golf vehicle, did you see this document?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Who was it who issued this document? What is the indication?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: The municipality of Sekovici, the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And now, in the same document, can we move on to the English page number 5 and B/C/S page number 5 as well? Could you please read what you see on the screen?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: I can see a sales-purchase agreement for a passenger vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have this document in your binder?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And who was the car sold to, according to this contract?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: According to this contract, the Golf was sold to the Zvornik bank based in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And before that, who did the Golf belong to?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: This Golf belonged to the command of the Zvornik Brigade and was used as an official vehicle for the command of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Micic, for your explanation. And now, do you have any other example of abuse that was committed by Mr. Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: I remember a tractor that he gave away to Boro Tadic [as interpreted], his father-in-law, as a gift. This was his wife's father.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like to call up document 1D400 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read a short paragraph to you, having heard that Lieutenant Dragan Obrenovic abused his official position and gave away a military tractor, IMT, and gave it as a gift to Boro Gajic from Kozluk, we started collecting and checking information. Mr. Micic, did you have this document in your collection of documents that were relative to the actions of Dragan Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened to the tractor?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: This tractor, once it was repaired and overhauled, the registration and chassis number was falsified and the tractor was sold on to Serbia to Zrenjanin municipality, if my memory serves me well.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And now something about Dragan Obrenovic's abuse of power when it came to property. Was Dragan Obrenovic involved in that as well?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you give us some more details? When did all this start?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: This type of abuse started, as far as I knew about the property crimes at the time, when he started building his family house in Zvornik. He was building it in a plot that the Zvornik municipality gave to Lieutenant Colonel Obrenovic free of charge as a well-deserving citizen. We are talking about a house that he was building. According to the information that we had and that was subsequently confirmed, when he was building this house, he used military vehicles to haul the building materials. He also used servicemen as work power, and he also gave them food from the military supplies. In other words, the troops were engaged to build his house and he fed the troops from the reserves or from the kitchen of the military unit that he was in command of.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Micic, could you please try and remember and tell us when this building plot was given to Mr. Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you the exact period of time or the date, but I personally participated in locating the land certificate from the cadastre of the Zvornik municipality. This document exists and I'm sure that you will be able to see it from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How was the building material obtained for the building of that particular house?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: Save for some of the building materials, such as the doors, the windows, we could not establish at the time how he obtained other building materials to build his family house.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up document 1D403 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Micic, are you familiar with this document? Did you see it among the documents that referred to the operative case Kum?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us briefly what this document refers to?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: This document is about the delivery of doors and windows from the company Metalano in Zvornik to the address of the military post in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What else did you learn about other illegal activities and property illegally obtained by Mr. Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: I remember a building device or a building equipment King, which at the time was also removed illegally from the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about this machine known as King? How long had it been in the Zvornik Brigade before that?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: At the time we established that this piece of equipment called King belonged to a building company or a construction company. As far as I remember the name of the company was Kamenolom which was the stone quarry at the entrance to Zvornik. The machine was pretty much neglected but nobody looked after it. The Zvornik Brigade had it at its disposal.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: While -- was the King machine also used during the war?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: While we still have the document on the screen, could you please tell us the date on the document? When was this invoice issued?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: The 26th June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Micic. Is there anything else you can tell us about any other cases of abuse?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: The commander of the Zvornik Brigade, Lieutenant Colonel Obrenovic, availed himself of the so-called war booty. He used about five tractors to fell trees and transport timber. He also engaged troops from his unit to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Micic, if there are no other details you can remember --

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember the building of a different family residence which was recorded as property of his mother in Sremska Mitrovica Stari Banovci settlement. I personally checked the status of that property.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How did you obtain all this information?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: We obtained the information in contact with the officers and the civilians from the unit and the area. We talked to the members of the unit who obviously were against the commander's ways, i.e., with his abuse. I would not have any comments to his work proper, i.e., to the command and control that he exercised.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In order to avoid going through all the documents starting with 1D390 to 1D422, which all refer to the information collected about the abuse of power by the commander of the Zvornik Brigade, I'm going to ask the witness some of my final questions. Mr. Micic, how did the whole operative case Kum end up?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: As I've already told you, I was temporarily assigned to this task and my assignment lasted for some 20 days. And the persons in charge of the investigation was the security organ of the 5th Corps and the security organ of the 503rd Motorised Brigade. They were the ones who were tasked with working on the case. And they continued working on the case when I left and was reassigned. I remember that no criminal charges were raised in respect of this case and that, after a certain while, Lieutenant Colonel Obrenovic was extradited to The Hague, so I can't tell you what the organ of the 5th Corps and the organ of the 503rd Brigade did in respect of this case once I left.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This operative case Kum did not involve just Obrenovic, did it?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: The operative case Kum was not only about Lieutenant Colonel Obrenovic personally. He was the most responsible person in the case. The whole case applied to a group of individuals, members of his unit, among whom he was the highest ranking officer and with him there was also a group of officers and civilians who participated in the matter and exercised different tasks upon his orders. I remember the chief of the technical services, a person -- a person who was in charge of the depot, and some other persons who were involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Micic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, and were criminal proceedings ever instituted in relation to these other persons or any other kind of proceedings? Disciplinary proceedings? Apart from Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I've just told you, I don't know whether any charges were raised against anybody with regard to this particular case, whether there was any disciplinary responsibility or anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Micic. Now, thank you, Madam Tapuskovic. Mr. Nikolic, do you wish to cross-examine this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. No questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Nikolic. Mr. Bourgon? Would you like to question this witness, cross-examine this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I do have a few questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Micic. My name is Stephane Bourgon and I'm counsel for Drago Nikolic in these proceedings. I have a very few questions for you and I would first like to ask you to look at a document which is 7DP176, if I can have the document in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, is there any list or anything that you may have sent us to alert us to this material?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon? I don't think Mr. Bourgon has --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, sorry, I was looking at that because I had the wrong document on my screen but this document was on the list of my colleague, Mr. Zivanovic, so there was no -- there was no problem of notice to the Prosecution. I just have a technical question that I would like to ask the witness about the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Simply, we don't have that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if it was on the list, it should be retrievable without any major difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It is on the screen, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it the one that we have on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It was on the other screen that I was looking for the document. It has two pages, to be able to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And do we have an English translation of it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it clear or is there agreement that it was on Mr. Zivanovic's list of documents to be used or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was on from the Prosecution list and this document was tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We've got a lot of those and it's not on any Defence lists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would object to the use of any documents at this point, unless he can make a foundation of why.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, this witness is coming to testify about Operation Kum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What is this document anyway?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just I'll be brief. This is a serious question of the rule of law. If they are going to be following these important rules, they need to follow them. If this is a document that he's just thought up now as cross sometimes happens, I have no objection. If this was a document that he'd been aware of, I certainly object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: (redacted). There is absolutely no problem, no reason why the Prosecution should not have prepared and be ready for me to ask a question related to this document this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think that answers my question. He's known about the document beforehand. He had the number to it, he gave us no notice, it appears, deliberately. If he says by accident he didn't, I'll have no objection. But if he's deliberately withholding a document he intends to use, he's got to follow the rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Our position is quite simple, actually. We are letting it go this time but legally, Mr. McCloskey is correct. The understanding and the directive of this Tribunal is that if you have documents that you intend to use for your cross-examination that you give information to your counterparts immediately before the cross-examination starts. Or at least -- exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I take good note of the Court's advice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would just like to say that concerning this document, I was not expecting to ask this question this morning related to the fact I thought it would be covered in the examination-in-chief, but now it comes out in the testimony, the issue of opening the mail, and I just want to follow up as a normal cross-examination. But I will take the guidance of the Court and apply it to the best of my ability, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: However, before my continue, my colleague just raised an issue that there might be something that needs to be redacted concern something that I may have said on the record earlier and I think I refer to page 45, at the end of page 45 which might need a redaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to redact the first three lines of Mr. Bourgon's intervention, starting at line 23 right through 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I suggest that to be safe 10 to 15 as well on that page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think it will be wise to do that. Thank you, Mr. Josse. 10 to 15, and then the first three lines, 23 to 25. Let's proceed. And there is the usual 30 minute delay in transmission. You may proceed, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Micic, if you look at the letter that is before you now in your language, I'd simply like to know if this, to your knowledge, is related to the incident that you mentioned in your testimony about the commander of the 503 Brigade opening mail which was addressed to the security organ of his brigade?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said so a moment ago that that particular instance to which this document relates has to do with the unlawful opening of the mail addressed to the security organ of the 503rd Brigade. It is therefore linked with that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in terms of timing, would this letter be before or after your arrival in the lines of the 503 Brigade to perform your duties in respect of Operation Kum?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: This event occurred before my arrival at the Zvornik Brigade to work there on a temporary basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I take it, Mr. Micic, that when you -- you've testified earlier that you did at one point confront Dragan Obrenovic with some allegations related to Operation Kum, but on the initial meeting you had at the brigade, that is in the company of Mr. Savic, I take it that at that particular time you did not inform Dragan Obrenovic that he was the target of the investigation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, correct. Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
