utterances.text: And are you familiar with the fact that following the -- both the mail incident and that first visit, that Obrenovic had ordered Savic to be replaced as chief of security and had appointed him as a liaison officer to foreign forces and that he wanted to replace him with Jasikovac as security officer? Are you familiar with this?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: Yes. I am familiar with this attempted removal. However, a commander of a unit may only in agreement with the chief of the security administration, effect appointments in lower units and I'm referring to the corps, brigade, regiment, battalion, wherever there were security organs present, without a decision from the chief of the security administration, such appointments could not be carried out in a legal way. Yes, I am familiar with this attempted removal of Dragoslav Savic. He was ultimately not removed from that position, continued working there and actively participating in my investigations until subsequently he stopped being a member of the VRS altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And Mr. Micic, how would you qualify, throughout these events that you were personally involved in, the reaction of Dragan Obrenovic, or the feelings of Dragan Obrenovic, to what you can tell, towards the security branch?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: Since I hadn't been discussing these issues with Lieutenant Colonel Obrenovic, I could only make my conclusions on the basis of his actions and behaviour. These conclusions were that he was worried for his own sake and his post, on account of the evidently unlawful activities he was engaged in, such as opening other people's mails, reassigning individuals elsewhere, his conduct toward Savic, and his attitude toward the group of people I worked with. This also went for the group of people surrounding him, whom he engaged in these activities with. His actions directly resulted in him being worried and concerned about possible criminal charges or disciplinary charges being brought against him, all of which led him to his attempts to eliminate those individuals who were potential witnesses and who could testify about these actions of his.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, would you agree with me, Mr. Micic, that an investigation such as Kum, regardless of the results of the investigation at the end, can have some major repercussions on the military career of any officer, especially a senior officer?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: Precisely so. I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And based on your experience, is it the type of investigation that may prevent a senior officer from being promoted to the next rank in a structure?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MICIC
utterances.text: It may, once it goes through the disciplinary proceedings before the competent disciplinary military court, which result in one of the penalties being the ban on any further promotions. The results can also be his dishonourable discharge from that particular post and reassignment to a lower-level post, one which he had been occupying before having committed abuse of office, if you understand me correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. And maybe just one last question. To your knowledge, is there any relationship between the fact that there was Operation Kum and the fact that Lieutenant Colonel Obrenovic was never promoted to a higher rank after the war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That misstates the evidence. If you recall, we have -- Major Obrenovic was the rank during our events, and so I think his -- the premise to his question is wrong. I don't recall precisely at this time the date of the promotion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, during the war, Dragan Obrenovic held the rank of major. Immediately following the war, not too long after, he was promoted to Lieutenant Colonel, while the commander of the brigade was promoted to colonel on the same day. That's the evidence on the record. My question is not this. My question is: Is there a relationship between these events, Kum, which happened later, and the fact that he was never promoted above Lieutenant Colonel. It's a completely different question and it's to the knowledge of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's totally speculative given the background.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Either the witness knows, has inside information on this. If he hasn't, he cannot speculate. Yes, Mr. Micic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only know that Lieutenant Colonel Obrenovic was Lieutenant Colonel at the time I was in charge of that case, and I was a Lieutenant Colonel at the time as well. I cannot answer that specific question because it falls within the purview of the personnel services at the level of the corps. I cannot tell if this had any bearing on his promotion or not. This was not within the extent of knowledge that I had at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Micic. I have no further questions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will soon have the break, but before we do so, I want to know where we stand. Mr. Gosnell, you will not be cross-examining this witness, will you?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: No, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Sarapa?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: No questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So, soon after the break -- you're not cross-examining the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Which means, Mr. Micic, that your testimony ends here, unless my colleagues wish to put questions to you. Thank you very much for having come over to give testimony and please have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll do the documents after the break. 25 minutes, because I have a meeting now. --- Break taken at 11.59 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Madam Tapuskovic, documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. A list has been submitted for the previous witness. Those are documents between 1D390 to 1D422.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'm objecting to all those based on the fact that the foundation was not laid. They didn't even ask the person if -- what the results of the investigation were, whether he was cleared, not cleared, clearly made no effort to even do that and without that effort to have been made minimally, I don't think these documents can mean anything to you. They, in fact, they specifically and deliberately apparently did not follow up on where this went. So in my view, with that lack of foundation, these documents should be given no weight at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any remark from the other Defence teams? Yes, Madam Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that at this moment, it is not that important whether the witness spoke about the outcome of every investigation that had been carried out. The documents were shown to him, he recognised them, and he spoke about their contents and he also explained what activities are described in each of these documents and he also confirmed that these activities had been undertaken during the investigation, so I believe that the documents are indeed relevant for the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. My colleague's argument was that these documents should be given no weight at all. That was on page 52, lines 23 and line 1 of page 53. This is unrelated to admissibility. This will be for the Trial Chamber to determine what weight will be given to these documents but for now they have probative value. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. Our decision is to admit these documents without, of course, prejudicing the weight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So as I said, without prejudice, of course, to submissions that can be made later on as to their weight, if at all. So that completes our testimony of Nebojsa Micic. Next witness? For the record, we have sitting in the row reserved for the Beara team, a gentleman whose name I don't know. This is following an agreement that there has been between the Prosecution and the Popovic Defence team. The gentleman will be assisting the next witness in the uploading and demonstration of some documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I was just going to introduce the gentleman, who is sitting with the Beara team. His name is Bozo Grbic, who will be assisting us during the examination of our witness. He is actually the assistant of Mr. Miladin Kovacevic who is our expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. You're about to start giving evidence as an expert witness for the Popovic Defence team. Before you do so, our rules require that you make a solemn declaration that you will be testifying the truth. The text is being handed to you now. Please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Madam Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kovacevic. For the record, I'm going to introduce myself to you. My name is Mira Tapuskovic, and I appear on behalf of Mr. Vujadin Popovic. I'm going to ask you to speak slowly, and before starting your answer, could you please check that my question has been recorded and also I'm not going to start asking my next question before you answer the previous one. This is necessary for the transcript and for the appropriate recording of everything that is being said in the courtroom. Mr. Kovacevic, could you please give us your name for the record?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Miladin Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where and when were you born?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 24th of August, 1952, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, municipality Gacko in the place call Kazanci.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I received -- we received your curriculum vitae which is Exhibit 1D1128. However, could you please tell us, Mr. Kovacevic, something about your educational background?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: My formal education background is as follows. I graduated from the school of natural sciences and mathematics in Belgrade with a degree in mathematics in 1976. After that, I enrolled in post-graduate studies at the University of Zagreb and I obtained a master's degree in economics, or, rather, in the area of statistics and this was in 1978. After that, I prepared my doctoral thesis and I obtained my PhD in mathematical statistics at the school of economics in Zagreb in 1983.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what about your professional career from the moment you graduated and later on?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In a nutshell, I am mostly involved with two areas of work. One is state statistics, i.e. public service, and the second is my academic career or teaching at university. I started by joining the institute for statistics of the then Federal Bureau of Statistics of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. Later on, I was even the director of that institute. At the same time, I was teaching at two faculties, the school of economics in Belgrade and the school of mathematics also in Belgrade. I first -- I started by dedicating my work to the statistical methodology, then I continued with demography. Later on, I embarked on all sorts of research, mostly of public opinion and market. And some 15 years or so or a bit later, I started being interested in macroeconomics and economics in general, and currently I'm at the position of the deputy of the director of the national bureau of statistics. I am the adviser of the national bank and I am also an associate researcher of the economic institute as a member of the editorial board of a magazine that writes about economic trends and economic policies.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kovacevic. When did you start working as an expert in the Defence team of Mr. Vujadin Popovic?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Approximately three years ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you prepared your expert report marked as 1D1129?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, in very brief outlines, and can you tell the Trial Chamber and our learned friends what documents were available to you when you started preparing your expert report?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I received documents successively starting with the moment when I embarked on my research. At first, I had nothing but the report and the annex to the report drafted by Mrs. Helge Brunborg and Mr. Henrik Urdal and then I received documents that consisted of certain written documents or electronic databases and so on and so forth. Some of those documents I used in the demographic department of the Tribunal. I'm talking about the databases which are not publicly accessible, and the most important databases were the 1991 census in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the list of voters dating back to 1977 and 1997 and 1998 in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the list of missing persons from the protected area of Srebrenica which was put together by the experts of the Tribunal, Brunborg and Urdal, and a few other documents such as the lists of members of the BiH army, databases of the displaced persons from the protected area of Srebrenica, the lists of -- I don't know, some other lists. I'm talking about rather ample documentation so I can't give all these documents to you off the cuff.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You've also told us that you worked here at the Tribunal in the demographic department. When was that? Who did you work with? And what was the outcome of your work here at the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I worked here on two Tribunal -- occasions, in the month of April, together with my colleagues who were IT specialists and especially those who are specialised in database searches, Mr. Bozo Grbic and Mr. Branko Jirecek were with me on the first occasion. On the second occasion I was working only with Mr. Bozo Grbic. The result of our searches and of our work has been fully described in my report, and actually it is mostly relative to the database searches, primarily the contrasting and matching of the lists of voters with the list of missing people.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So the result of your researches has been involved in your work but how are the data that you analysed during your work at the demographic unit of the Tribunal stored?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The data are stored electronically, according to the protocol and as such they are available at the Tribunal and available to the Tribunal staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Listing the documents that you used to prepare your report, you mentioned the list of missing persons. You also mentioned Brunborg's consolidated list of missing persons. Did you use any other lists that were available to you?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: We used the lists that were used to put the consolidated list together, primarily, the ICRC and PMR [as interpreted] list. We also used the list of voters and the census.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What is the difference between the two lists that you have just mentioned? The first one being the ICRC list and the second being the PHR list, both of which were at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: These lists were generated in the following way. The ICRC list, according to Brunborg and Urdal report, applied to all the victims in Bosnia and Herzegovina, actually to all the people missing from Bosnia and Herzegovina whereas the PHR list referred only to the protected area of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So your conclusion was what? How did the consolidated report come about and how do you call that list that you used in your report?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: We are talking about the consolidated report based on the previously mentioned two lists, although there are some other sources mentioned in the Brunborg and Urdal's report. There is a consolidated list which was the result of a fusion of the two lists. With the selection of those missing persons that would refer to the protected area of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Since you have gone through Brunborg's work and the consolidated list of Helge Brunborg and his associate, could you briefly describe the procedure underlying the consolidated list relative to the dead and missing from the area of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In a nutshell, Urdal and Brunborg, first carried out a fusion of the two aforementioned lists and ended up with one consolidated list and then they checked, i.e., embarked on a process to check the credibility of that list. First, they wanted to establish for every person listed in the list whether that person had existed in respect of the benchmark census from 1991. And second of all, they wanted to establish whether that person is possibly among the living, and they did it by comparing and contrasting the names with the census list from 1997 and 199 -- 1997 and 1998. So these are the two lists that were compiled by the competent organisations and the credibility was checked by contrasting the census of 1991 and list of voters from 1997 and 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If I can conclude from your explanation by matching the lists with the census, what purpose was achieved?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The purpose that was achieved was to establish the credibility from the aspect of the realistic or physical existence of a person during the census that was carried out in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what about matching with the list of voters from 1997 and 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The process of matching with the 1997 and 1998 list of voters was aimed at verifying for each and every person on the consolidated list, whether they are registered in the list of voters that were compiled in 1997 and 1998. That was a guarantee that the person on the list was indeed missing, if their names did not appear in the 1997 and 1998 lists.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you were checking the reliability of these lists, what was your approach to the verification of credibility and trustworthiness?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: When it came to the trustworthiness of the list of missing that was compiled by Brunborg and Urdal was on the one hand to reconstruct the process of matching of that list with the census and the list of voters; and on the other hand, I was looking at the ratio between the number of missing on the list with cross matching with other sources of data and the balance relations that were obtained on those data sources, i.e., the documents that mentioned any data either referring to the number of the population, the number of missing, the number of identified and some other figures.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Does it mean that in one way or another, you repeated the matching process that you went over the same grounds that Brunborg and his associate had already done?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I actually performed the IT processing of the data, which implied the matching of the list with the census and the -- also with the list of voters.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You have told us that you also performed the matching with the 1991 census. What is the connection between that particular list and you?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: At the time, I was the head of the department for demographics at the then-federal bureau of statistics. I was in charge of the last census in Yugoslavia which also included Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During his work on compiling the consolidated list and comparing it with the census of 1991, Helge Brunborg used the so-called keys, a total of 71 of them, in order to establish a connection between the persons on the list of missing and the list of persons from the 1991 census. What would be your view of those rules and what would be your comments?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The 71 keys that you're talking about had been constructed as the ID surrogate which starts from principal ID key that connects of the first name, the family name, the father's name, the sex, the date of birth and the place of birth. These rules were designed in order to select the narrow groups from the census, where a certain pair could be found, on the one hand a person from the list of missing could be found in that group in case when the ID keys are not identical between the census and the list of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In order to simplify things for us, in order to explain to us the whole ID process that was undertaken, can you give us an example? We don't have to have the whole list of missing persons. In your report, you have several tables with several names. Could you please take a random name from any of the tables? For example, on page 15 of your expert report, this is quite an indicative table, and could you please give us an example of -- I'm talking about paragraph 49, Mr. Kovacevic. Could you give us an example which will show us how the 71 keys were used by Mr. Brunborg?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The table or the illustration in paragraph 49 does not refer to the census but, rather, to the list of identified persons, and the procedure is described how the list of identified persons was processed but when it comes to the census, I can explain how any individual in the census was compared in order to find a matching pair between the census and the list of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Give us an example.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: An example of that so it might be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just a moment. Ms. Soljan?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, just one point I wanted to make. When we refer to the list of missing, it might be helpful to refer whether it's the OTP list of missing, the ICRC list of missing or the PHR list of missing because they may create confusion in the record. So, for the clarity of the record, to understand which list of missing is being dealt with right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Soljan. Yes, Ms. Tapuskovic. I think you can clarify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, you heard the question. Was the list -- or is the list of the dead and the missing that you're referring to the one that was made by the ICRC or is it the list made by Helge Brunborg?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: From the outset we have been referring to the consolidated list of missing made by Brunborg and Urdal which was in fact a fusion of two lists, one of which was made by the ICRC and the other one was made by the organisation Medecins Sans Frontieres, or what was it called?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Physicians for Human Rights?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, right, Physicians for Human Rights.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, let us go back to the question that was put to you earlier. Can you give us an illustration with an invented name and the possible information that the consolidated list could provide in order to show us how the matching was done through the application of the 71 rules or keys invented by Mr. Brunborg?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, here we can see in my report a part of the list of missing persons which was the result of the comparison of that list with the list of voters. That's paragraph 26. For instance, let us have a look at it just to have an idea of it. We can take any person. For instance, under 2: Hadzic, Omer, Mujo, that's to say last name Hadzic, father's name Omer, name, Mujo; municipality of residence, Srebrenica; municipality of birth, Vlasenica; and then we have the year of birth, since we lack the data concerning the day and month of birth. These is the information from Brunborg's list. According to Brunborg and Urdal, this is how the matching was done. Let me just state here that the part of the matching that has to do with the automatic computer processing is something that we repeated, we did, re-did, that's to say. So then we have the name, father's name, municipality of residence, well, in this case my apologies because the municipality of residence was taken over from the census. Then we have the municipality of birth, and the year of birth, once we have this individual, it is -- matches are attempted to be found in the census based on these keys. If there is no match, then this individual is the subject of searches according to the 71 criteria we mentioned. This is how the procedure goes. We take the most rigorous criterion and then we go down to the least rigorous criterion, thus the individual is tracked down according to one of the criteria. Let's take criterion number 42, which is the lease rigorous criterion and I've chosen it now deliberately. The identification elements are, initials, that's to say the first letter of the name, father's name, the first letter of the surname, year of birth, but a relaxed year of birth, which means that what is sought is an interval of plus/minus three years around the year of birth that is found in the list of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In order to make this more easier for us to understand, you should firstly speak more slowly and secondly, please tell us, you've taken this example of Mirsad Salihovic?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I took this other example, Omer Hadzic but it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Hadzic, Mujo, father's name Omer, from Srebrenica. If we take this individual, how would this individual be matched according to this 42nd key or which ever other key you use and what sort of datum would be sought?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Since such an individual was not found in the census, not with the identical elements we have in the list of missing persons, that is, we found an individual with the family name Hadzic, father's name Omer, first name Mujo, municipality of birth Vlasenica, and year of birth 1928, 71 criteria were applied, each one of them being a certain reduction of the identification elements so that, for instance, the individual can be found among a group of individuals who stand out according to, for instance, criterion 42 or any other criterion. But let's take criterion 42 for the sake of an illustration. This would mean that such an individual could be found among individuals whose name is -- whose name starts with the letter H, so the initial letter of their last name -- or, rather, of their first name, let's say, would match the initial of Mujo's first name and whose initial letter of the family name is H, and thus is a match with Hadzic, whose father's name according to this criterion matches the father's name of the individual from the list, and whose year of birth, with the possible range of plus-minus three years corresponds to 1928. So these could be individuals born in 1928 -- rather 1926, 27 or 29 or 1930. So this would be the criterion based on which a group of individuals would be selected and which would constitute a given match with the individual who is the subject of that search.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us clarify this. The piece of data you receive from the census, for instance, under the 71 keys, should that individual always have a full name, name and last name, or are initials enough?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In the list of missing persons, all the individuals have their first and last name, father's name, perhaps I'm not -- I'm not quite sure but let's say most of them have the municipality of birth cited and the year of birth as well, although a good many of them don't have a full date of birth cited in the list. For this reason, I'm directing your attention to the table in paragraph 26 where we have just an illustration of 22 individuals from that list. The table does not really serve the purpose of my explanation here. It just serves to show how the list of missing persons looked like.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In applying these 71 keys, when you use certain keys and don't use others, does this mean that you increase or decrease possibilities of finding the father's name, first name, last name, of the person, of the individual, on the list?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The possibility you get is that from a very wide circle of individuals from the census, you select a number of individuals who match the individuals in the list of missing persons. Let's look at illustration 1, which gives the numbers of groups which, according to these rules, may be used to search for individuals from the list of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, we will get to that later. Let us take it in the proper order in the way you put it in your report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Slow down, both of you, please, Mr. Kovacevic, and counsel. It's very -- please, all you need to do is allow a short pause between question and answer but you're moving a little bit too fast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up document 1D1129.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, appearing on your screen will be your report uploaded in e-court. Let's turn to the page where you describe the application of the 71 criteria. That's page 6 of the B/C/S version and page 5 of the English version, the table continues on page 6. Let us be quite specific, Mr. Kovacevic. This table, the first vertical column is where you entered the numbers of the criteria applied by Mr. Brunborg; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So in that column, you did not enter the parameters contained in each of the criteria?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No, because that's something that exists already in writing.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The table we see on our screens now contains figures that were the result of what sort of work and research done on your part?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: We repeated the process of matching as was previously done by Brunborg and Urdal for the purposes of identifying persons from the list of missing persons with corresponding persons from the census.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the total of five columns, one of which has the heading, "Rule," and the remaining four contain reference documents you used for comparison; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No. These were not reference documents. These were -- you mean the contents of the columns? Let's take column 2, which says, "1991 census all matches." Refers to the numbers of matches found in the census in respect of all the matches of all the persons from the missing list according to specific rules. Under rule 1, there were 522 such individuals. In the second row -- in the second column, a reduction was made of the number of matches in such a way that every person from the census which was matched to the list of missing was kept by eliminating the duplicates. So we have 522 persons from the census were found with corresponding matches in the list of missing persons, but, for instance, under rule 16, the total number of matches from the list of missing persons and the census list was 1750, but this number has 1736 different individuals from the census. In some other cases, the difference increases and the difference increases evidently as the reduction entailed by the rule increases, or depending on how rigorous the rule applied is. The third column also shows the result of the matches made --

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we pause there, Mr. Kovacevic, to first of all explain the two columns which evidently refer only to the census, because the third and fourth columns relate to the lists of voters. Can you explain why, according to the matches and comparisons you made, when rule 1 was applied, the number of matches found according to all the parameters found was identical to the number in the second column where only one match was made?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Matches were made only once -- or matching was made only once in both columns. The first column -- and I'm referring to this column saying, "1991 census all matches," that column contains the total number of matches from the census and the list of missing persons, regardless of the fact whether one person is -- appears several times among the matches. Now, the second column reduces that number to only the number -- the number of different persons, without any duplicates. In the case of the application of rule 1, the number is the same and that's because rule 1 is the most rigorous one. There could have been some duplicates but apparently there were none.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain the occurrence of a situation in which one person from the list of Helge Brunborg is matched with several other persons on the census?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It's really simple. If the rule is not strict enough, for example rules 41, 42 and some others are not, and if it only calls for the matching of the initials of the first and last name and the year of birth, within an interval of plus/minus three years, then any given person from the list of missing will yield a larger number of matches from the census, which will match in all the details.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, you've given us an example featuring only the initials or the year of birth plus/minus three years. Is this the same example that you explained a couple of minutes ago and said that the matching was done in the same way?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the same example although there are some other examples of the sort. There is actually a number of such examples here.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And now tell me whether the same principle, i.e., the application of the 71 criteria, was used and applied to another type of list, or was it only used to match the lists with the census? Did Helge Brunborg do that?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to establishing the trustworthiness of the consolidated list of missing that we are talking about all this time, the 71 criteria were used only in matching the list of missing and the census. It was not used, for example, to do the matching between the list of missing and the list of voters.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have an explanation why this wasn't done by Helge Brunborg? Why weren't the 71 criteria applied on the list of voters also?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The explanation provided by Brunborg in his report was that the list of voters do not contain the name of father. However, in a large number of cases, the name of father could have been transported from the census based on the established pairs, i.e. the persons who were identified in the list of missing in the census. We, on our part, did that, and I can tell you something about that later. I can only guess or speculate based on what we did. We did the matching between the list of missing and the list of voters, and we had a large number of individuals who appeared and who were identified by the application of these rules and who could be matched with the persons in the list of missing. But then we would have found ourselves in a situation where we would have to explain the reasons and explanations as to why none of these persons were accepted as matching persons in the list of missing, unlike in the case of comparison with the census where almost every individual on the list of missing could be found in the census, not all of them but a large majority of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you carried out your matching process, you said that you were able to find a few individuals could not be matched. Tell me, when you performed your matching between the list of missing and the census, how many such cases were there that no match could be found?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: There were 57 such cases altogether. In other words, 57 individuals from the list of missing could not be matched with the census or to the conservative criteria or the broadened criteria.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that irrespective of the strictness of the criteria that were applied, such persons could not be matched with anybody from the census?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: We cannot say with any degree of reliability that none of the 57 persons existed in any groups of individuals that were established for the purpose of matching according to the set of criteria or whether all the individuals were rejected as possible paths for the given person based on all the 71 criteria.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In your report, you state that during the process of matching, there was another problem, which was the location match when comparison was carried out with the census. What do you mean by the term "identical location"?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In Brunborg and Urdal's report, the matching with the census is described, and it says in one place that a match was rejected if the location was not identical, i.e., when the location did not match.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you talking about paragraph 9 of your report?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Precisely. This is exactly what I've been looking for. Yes. It says, and I quote, "And the meaning is the same, match between the missing persons list and the list of voters was rejected if the locations were not identical and the term, location, is not explained but only two possibilities may be allowed. One is the place of birth, and the other is the place of residence as recorded on the list of voters which could also be identified with the place from which the person went missing in the list of missing because in the strictest sense of the word, the place of residence does -- is not identical to the place from which the person went missing or disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain the -- how the data should look like in order to yield a perfect match?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: For example, if a person in the list of missing persons matches a person in the census according to the following criteria: The first name, the family name, the father's name, the date of birth, or perhaps the place of birth, and the only difference may be the place of disappearance in the list of missing as compared to the place of residence in the list of census. This would be a sufficient criteria to consider that there is no match, i.e., that the person in the list of missing does not have a match in the census.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You've just told us that matching with the list of voters implies that the person is still living at the moment when the list was compiled. Does this mean that such a matching process cannot lead to a conclusion that the person whom you try to match is still alive?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: This is a criterion which eliminates the possibility that the person from the list of missing is present on the list of voters, i.e., alive in 1997 or 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to the document that we currently have on the screen, and can we please look at the third and fourth columns? And could you try and explain for us the figures that appear in these two columns?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Once the father's name has been transported from the census into the list of voters, by using a key that we called the identification number or the JMBG as a specific personal identifier, so the father's name was transported from the census, from the missing person list to the list of voters, then we did the matching procedure following Brunborg's rules between the list of missing persons and the list of voters. This is the part of the automatic procedure that was not done by Brunborg and Urdal with an explanation that the fathers's name was missing from the list of voters.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. How did you resolve that problem?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I just explained, and let me repeat: We used the unique identifier, which we called the citizens number, we transported the name of father from the missing person's list to the list of voters. So that a very large number of individuals in the list of voters received the father's name according to the census where the father's name exists.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now go back to the text of your report? Let's go to paragraph 5, which is on page 1 in B/C/S version and on page 2 in the English version of the report. You say in this paragraph that the data in the list is not complete and you mention a unique identifier?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: A unique identifier.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What is it? What is the unique identifier?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: A unique identifier is a combination of elements, identifying elements, which allows for unique matches to be found for certain individuals who are mentioned on various lists. There are two unique identifiers in the case at hand. One I've already mentioned and that's the personal identification number held by every citizen and to be found in all the ID documents, such as identity card, passport, driver's licence and so on. Where this particular unique identifier does not exist, the other unique identifier is a combination of the following elements: Name, last name, father's name, date of birth, place of birth, and the sex. Where we have all these elements in respect of an individual, it is impossible to find a match for two persons who would have all these different elements met.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us why is the element of sex important in that combination?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: That particular aspect of the unique identifier -- or rather the particular aspect of the unique identifier is that it must point to one person only. It is important in view of the fact that back in our parts, there are names that -- first names that can be both names for women and men. For instance, Sava, that could be a woman's or man's name and that's why it's important to have the element of gender in that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If these two individuals are different, they have to have two different personal identification numbers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Personal identification numbers are designated always for one person and in such a way that they can designate one person and one person alone.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We still have eight minutes left before we adjourn for the day. Let me draw your attention to paragraph 6 of your report, which is page 2 of the Serbian version, and page 2 of the English version, where you mention the fact that there are -- that there is no information about the last place of residence, both in the ICRC list and in the PHR lists. What is the significance of this, that these lists --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Should also contain the last place of residence in addition to everything else.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: That particular piece of information about the last place of residence or the last place of permanent residence is something that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter isn't sure if the witness said that it misses from the list or is on the list.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation]... of both the ICRC and PHR and consequently did not find its way in the consolidated Brunborg-Urdal list and it's very important if you want to match the census against the list of voters because voters' lists contain as a rule that bit of information as does the census.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can I stop you there, sir, because we have a problem in the interpretation. Can you please repeat your answer to my question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He only needs to repeat, to clear a part of it, to clarify. In giving your answer to the previous question, Mr. Kovacevic, were you referring to when someone is missing from the list or to someone who is on the list of the ICRC and PHR?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was referring to the persons that are on the lists, either those of the ICRC or PHR's lists or on the Brunborg consolidated list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's clear enough now. I think you can move to your next question, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In your report, table 1 referred to the lists of voters from 1997 and 1998. Tell us what do you know, if anything at all, about the lists of voters in Bosnia-Herzegovina toward the very end of these events in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in the aftermath of the war there?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the voters lists used by Urdal and Brunborg, from the elections back in 1997 and 1998, I know that there were elections held in 1996. To tell you the truth, I don't know whether they were parliamentary or local elections. At any rate there had to have existed lists of voters in 1996 as well. This begs the question of why those lists were not taken into consideration as well, since they were closer to the time period of these events.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any explanation for the fact that these lists were not used?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have finished one area and since we only have two to three minutes left, I should perhaps leave my next topic for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Madam. That's exactly what we will do. Mr. Kovacevic, you will need to return tomorrow for the continuation of your testimony. I'm not that sure that we will finish tomorrow but we will do our best.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, one important rule that applies to you as a witness who has still not finished his testimony, it's important that between now and when you resume your testimony tomorrow, you do not communicate with anyone on the subject matter of your testimony. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for informing me. It's quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So we'll reconvene tomorrow morning at 9 -- no, tomorrow afternoon, tomorrow afternoon, there is no chance of moving it to the morning any of these three days, no?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Tomorrow afternoon, at 2.15. Thank you.
